area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain, demonstrate from the right seat and teach a normal and crosswind takeoff and climb at VY ±5 knots, predict the day's takeoff performance with a learner, and spot, explain and fix the takeoff errors learners make most.
why: About one in five general aviation accidents happens during takeoff and departure climb, and more than half of those come from some failure of the pilot [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Every learner you send solo must first be trained in normal and crosswind takeoffs [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(d)(3)]], and what a learner learns first sticks hardest, so these early lessons set habits for a whole flying career [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

prereading.what: Normal and crosswind takeoff, the instructor notes inside them, ground effect, VX and VY, rejected takeoff, noise abatement.
prereading.label: AFH 6-1 to 6-14

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance, telling-and-doing, positive exchange of flight controls, sterile flight deck, use of distractions.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-10

prereading.what: Runway surface and slope, hydroplaning, and how weight, wind, speed and density altitude change takeoff distance.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-12 to 11-16

prereading.what: Building and adjusting personal minimums for wind and runway length.
prereading.label: RMH 2-4 to 2-5

prereading.what: Engine failure after takeoff and why a turn back is not for learners.
prereading.label: AFH 18-7 to 18-8

prereading.what: Wake vortex strength, behavior near the ground and avoidance on departure.
prereading.label: AIM 7-4-1 to 7-4-6

prereading.what: Line up and wait, and how to stay out of a runway incursion.
prereading.label: AIM 5-2-5

warmup: Think first: your learner's first three takeoffs all end the same way. The nose jerks up right after lift-off and the airspeed sags 8 knots below VY. Is the problem in the learner's hands, eyes or understanding? How could you find out before you say a word about it?

key_terms.def: A way to teach a skill in four phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
The flight version of demonstration-performance. Its key step is the learner telling while the instructor does, before the learner flies [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
What is learned first makes a strong, almost unshakable impression, so the instructor must teach it right the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
A three-step spoken handoff ('You have the flight controls,' 'I have the flight controls,' 'You have the flight controls') with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Gradual back-elevator pressure that raises the nosewheel slightly off the runway to set the lift-off attitude [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
Best angle of climb speed: the greatest altitude gain for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Best rate of climb speed: the greatest altitude gain per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Better performance very close to the ground, normally up to one wingspan high, from reduced induced drag [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. The airplane performs as if it were at that altitude [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].
A pilot's own limits, such as the most crosswind or the shortest runway they will accept, built from experience and comfort level [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].
Small bounces while the crosswind pushes the airplane sideways on the takeoff roll. It puts severe side loads on the landing gear [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
The false feeling of a nose-up attitude caused by rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff, when visual references are poor [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: The maneuver and the standard you hold

body.p: A takeoff is one continuous maneuver, but you teach it in three parts: the takeoff roll, the lift-off and the initial climb. The initial climb ends at a safe maneuvering altitude or when an en route climb is set up [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

A normal takeoff is made into the wind. The headwind gives some airspeed before you even move, and it cuts the groundspeed needed to fly, so the roll is shorter and the gear takes less wear [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. The POH/AFM sets the speeds and configuration; when it differs from the handbook, the manufacturer wins [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

head: Item
Private ACS (your learner)
Flight Instructor ACS (you)
rows: Climb pitch after lift-off
Recommended speed or VY, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S11)
Recommended speed or VY, ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.A.S12)
Climb to safe maneuvering altitude
VY +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S13)
VY ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.A.S14)
Rotation
At the recommended airspeed, then accelerate to VY (ACS PA.IV.A.S9)
Same, while you explain it aloud (ACS AI.VII.A.S11)

body.p: Your ACS adds a second job: you demonstrate and explain at the same time, and you analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VII.A Skills). If no crosswind exists on test day, the examiner tests the crosswind elements orally (ACS AI.VII.A Note).

callout.text: The ideal lift-off attitude needs only small pitch changes after lift-off to reach VY [[24:136|AFH 6-4]]. If your own picture is solid, flying ±5 knots while talking is easy. If it is not, the talking will show it.

check.q: Your learner's VY is 74 knots. What windows apply to the learner on a private checkride and to you on the CFI checkride?
check.a: Learner: 69 to 84 knots (+10/-5, ACS PA.IV.A.S13). You: 69 to 79 knots (±5, ACS AI.VII.A.S14).

chunks.title: Air, weight, wind and surface: what changes the numbers

body.p: Thin air hurts three ways: less engine power, less propeller thrust and less lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. High density altitude means longer takeoff rolls and weaker climbs [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. At altitude you lift off at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level, but at a higher true airspeed, so the roll gets longer [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

head: Change
Effect on takeoff
Source
rows: 10% more weight
About 5% faster lift-off, at least 9% slower acceleration, at least 21% longer distance
Headwind of 10% of takeoff speed
About 19% shorter distance
Lift-off 10% faster than the POH speed
About 21% longer distance (distance goes with speed squared)
Upsloping runway
Slower acceleration, longer ground run
Downsloping runway
Faster acceleration, shorter takeoff

body.p: Tailwind: a tailwind of 10% of takeoff airspeed adds about 21% to takeoff distance, because the airplane needs more groundspeed to reach lift-off airspeed [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. A tailwind takeoff is sometimes needed, but first confirm the POH/AFM approves it and that performance and runway are enough [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

Takeoff surface/condition: chart numbers assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway. Grass, gravel, dirt, potholes, mud, snow and standing water all slow acceleration [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Rough, soft or muddy fields each call for a slightly different technique than a hard runway [[24:136|AFH 6-4]]. Wet pavement also hurts the abort: hydroplaning tires give almost no braking or steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]], and hydroplaning starts at about 9 times the square root of tire pressure in knots [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

callout.text: Teaching tip: before solo, tell the learner the airplane will lift off earlier and climb faster without your weight, and the climb picture will look different. If it surprises them, the anxiety can last into a poor landing [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

check.q: A learner says, 'I'll lift off 10% fast for safety on this short strip.' What does that do to the takeoff distance?
check.a: Adds about 21%, since distance varies with the square of takeoff speed [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. On a critical runway that can be prohibitive.

chunks.title: Choosing the runway: performance, distance and the pilot

callout.text: Before every flight the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, or other reliable data for elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Airplane performance and limitations: before going to the airplane, check the POH/AFM charts and decide whether a safe takeoff and climb is possible here today [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Chart data come from a new airplane flown with average skill; adjust for a worn airplane or weaker skills [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

Teach interpolation with Figure 11-21: for 2,500 feet at 20 °C, average the 2,000-foot and 3,000-foot ground rolls, (1,115 + 1,230) / 2 = 1,173 feet [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. Rounding toward the more adverse value gives a small safety margin [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. Notice the conditions box: flaps 10°, full throttle before brake release, paved level runway, zero wind.

Available distance: your numbers must fit the runway, and an abort needs room too. Takeoff ground roll plus landing ground roll is a good estimate of the runway needed to accelerate and stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Declared distances can be more or less than the painted runway [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]]. If you want full length instead of an intersection, tell ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10]].

Wind: when the wind is 5 knots or more, ATC assigns the runway most nearly aligned with it, and tailwind and crosswind come before noise or delay programs. If you want another runway, say so [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]]. Airplanes are shown controllable in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO, and newer ones placard the demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

Pilot capability: the airplane's limit is not the learner's limit. The RMH sample personal minimums list a 7-knot crosswind component and a 2,500-foot shortest runway for a single-engine pilot [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. For special conditions such as an unfamiliar airport, fatigue or outside pressures, it suggests extra margins such as adding at least 500 feet to runway length and subtracting at least 5 knots from winds [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. One RMH pilot keeps a 20% margin over calculated takeoff distance [[30:32|RMH 3-14]].

callout.text: Personal minimums are not changed to make a flight happen. Change one variable at a time, and only after training with a flight instructor [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. That instructor is you.

check.q: Using Figure 11-21, what ground roll does the table give at 4,000 feet pressure altitude and 30 °C, and what total distance to clear 50 feet?
check.a: 1,465 feet ground roll and 2,790 feet total [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

head: Climb
What it gives
When
rows: VX
Most altitude for the distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Clearing obstacles such as trees or power lines off a short field [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]
VY
Most altitude for the time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Departing a runway with no obstructions until safe to change to a cruise climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
Cruise (normal) climb
Better cooling, control authority and view over the nose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
After a safe altitude, per the POH

body.p: VX is usually a little slower than VY, and both come from the POH/AFM [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. As altitude goes up, VX increases and VY decreases until they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Weight, altitude, gear and flaps all cut excess power, so both climbs get worse, and a heavier airplane needs a higher speed for its best rate [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

Why the ACS is strict: in some airplanes a 5-knot error costs a lot of climb [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. And VY is not free: it needs a much quicker pilot response to a power failure to avoid a stall, so the AFH suggests considering a lower-pitch cruise climb [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Ground effect, normally up to one wingspan high, cuts induced drag [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. It also makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter read a little low. Climbing out of it, the airplane needs more angle of attack, has more induced drag, tends to pitch up, and the airspeed reading rises [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

callout.text: In ground effect the airplane may seem able to fly below the recommended speed. Climbing out too slow gives much less climb than VY or even VX, and at high density altitude or max weight it may not climb out at all [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

check.q: A learner asks why we climb at VY after a normal takeoff instead of VX. Your short answer?
check.a: VY gives the most altitude in the least time, which is what you want when no obstacle needs a steep angle [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. VX is for clearing obstacles [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

chunks.title: Configuration: flaps, trim, prop, mixture, gear

bullets: Flaps: POH/AFM flap guidance for takeoff is precise, because it is based on climb performance. Never exceed the POH flap setting for takeoff [[24:236|AFH 12-5]]. Retract flaps and gear once a positive rate of climb is established [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Trim: if the airplane is trimmed for takeoff, the elevator tends to center as speed builds [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. Some back pressure may still be needed after lift-off until climb speed is reached [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Constant-speed propeller: low pitch, high rpm for takeoff lets the engine make maximum power [[24:237|AFH 12-6]]. The tach should come up to within 40 rpm of red line at full power and stay there [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].
Mixture: at high-elevation airports the mixture may be too rich during the runup; lean it [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

Retractable gear: normally retract when you could no longer land on the runway if the engine quit. Plan it for runway length, climb gradient, obstacles, terrain past the end and your airplane's climb [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

body.p: Power: keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above the surrounding terrain or obstacles. VY plus takeoff power gives the most altitude in the least time to handle an emergency [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Then set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

callout.text: Watch a learner reach for the gear handle: leaning forward can push the yoke and start a descent. And never retract before a positive rate shows on the instruments [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

check.q: Your learner suggests one more notch of flaps than the POH lists 'to get off sooner.' Your answer?
check.a: No. The POH takeoff flap setting is based on climb performance and must never be exceeded [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

chunks.title: Before the roll: checklists, radios, runway and wind

bullets: Checklists: finish run-up and before-takeoff items before taxiing onto the runway. Engine instruments normal; controls full, free and correct [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Do the items, then use the checklist to confirm, and model a positive attitude toward checklists [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

Radio: at a towered field get the takeoff clearance before taxiing onto the runway; at a nontowered field announce on CTAF [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Say the airport name at the start and end of each call, and never say 'active runway' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. Example: 'Frederick traffic, Cessna 801TF departing runway one niner' [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].
Verify the runway: set the heading bug to the runway heading and, before adding power, check that heading and runway agree [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

Wind: the large end of a wind cone or sock points into the wind, as does the cross bar of a wind tee. Don't use a tetrahedron for wind direction [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]]. A sock also shows speed and gusts [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. No indicator? Use smoke, dust, brush fires, wind farms or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Controls for wind: quartering headwind, upwind aileron up. Quartering tailwind, elevator down and upwind aileron down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. On lineup, check the sock again; if there is a crosswind, start the roll with full aileron into the wind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

Clear and align: make sure the approach and takeoff paths are clear, then line up and pick references aligned with the runway, like centerline marks, lights, distant trees or towers [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

body.p: How to teach it: have the learner say each item aloud as they do it. Talking it through shows you whether an error is a misunderstanding or just hands that are not trained yet [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: At a nontowered field the tetrahedron points one way and the wind sock another. Which do you trust for wind, and why?
check.a: The wind sock. Pilots are cautioned against using a tetrahedron to judge wind direction; it shows landing direction [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]], and a tee or tetrahedron can be set by hand [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

chunks.title: Fly it and explain it: the normal takeoff

body.p: On the checkride you fly from the right seat and talk at the same time. Below, each step has what you do and a short line to say.

head: Step
What you do
What you say
rows: Power
Release brakes, advance throttle smoothly and continuously to takeoff power; toes on the rudders, not the brakes [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
'Smooth power, feet off the brakes.'
Gauges
Check engine instruments for a malfunction during the roll [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
'Rpm and oil pressure good, airspeed alive.'
Track
Rudder against torque and P-factor; aileron into any crosswind; no braking to steer [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
'Right rudder to hold the centerline; eyes far down the runway.'
Feel
Controls firm up as speed builds; smaller rudder inputs are needed [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
'Feel the pressure build: it is flying more than taxiing.'
Rotate
Gradual back pressure to raise the nosewheel slightly to the lift-off attitude; hold it until it flies [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
'Ease the nose up to this picture and hold it.'
Lift-off
Wings level, rudder for coordination, hold the pitch that accelerates to VY, trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
'Wings level, hold the attitude, let it accelerate.'
Climb
Pitch on the horizon, hold, then glance at airspeed; repeat as needed [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
'Attitude first, then the airspeed check.'
Track out
Keep two points ahead in line on the extended centerline [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]
'Those two points stay lined up.'
Level off power
Takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain, then climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
'500 above the trees, climb power, trim.'

body.p: Demonstrate the attitude for VY and have the learner memorize it. Expect a new learner to hold too much back pressure just after lift-off and pitch up abruptly [[24:136|AFH 6-4]]. Forcing the airplane off early can settle it back or stall it; letting the nose drop too far can also settle it [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. The climb pitch is lower when the airplane is heavy or density altitude limits power [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Noise abatement: procedures come from the Chart Supplement, local publications, handouts and the tower, and hold-position signs may remind you. If you don't know a procedure, ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

callout.text: Attitude, hold, check: set the picture on the horizon, hold it, then glance at the airspeed. Inertia makes the airspeed lag [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: Why does the AFH want the learner to judge the takeoff roll by control feel rather than by the airspeed indicator?
check.a: The feel of resistance shows controllability, not speed. The learner should sense the pressures and the airplane's response, using outside references [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

chunks.title: Crosswind takeoff: build it on what they know from taxiing

body.p: Crosswind: it affects the takeoff much as it affects taxiing, and the correction closely parallels taxi technique [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. That is a ready-made known-to-unknown lesson: start from the taxi control positions the learner already uses [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: Start the roll with full aileron into the wind. The raised upwind aileron pushes that wing down so it does not lift [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Expect less early performance: the deflected controls add drag [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Rudder keeps you straight, usually downwind rudder against weathervaning. P-factor's left yaw helps in a right crosswind and adds to the problem in a left one [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
As speed builds, use just enough aileron to keep the wings level, but keep some in the whole roll [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
The downwind main wheel may lift first. That is acceptable and better than side-skipping [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
In a significant crosswind, hold the mains on slightly longer, then make a smooth but very definite lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

Once climbing, turn the nose into the wind, level the wings and crab along the extended centerline. Check the ground track often; the wind can change a lot within a few hundred feet of the ground [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

body.p: What you watch for: a rising upwind wing exposes more wing to the wind and can start skipping, small bounces that turn into side-skipping and can break the gear [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. Also watch for too much aileron late in the roll, which leaves a steep bank into the wind at lift-off [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

callout.text: Teach the learner to judge sideways position from the runway, not to hold a fixed aileron amount. 'Mechanical' aileron use is one of the listed crosswind errors [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

check.q: Wind from the left, learner rolling with the yoke neutral. What will you see, and what do you say?
check.a: The left (upwind) wing starts to rise and the airplane may skip and drift [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. Say: 'Full left aileron, into the wind,' then ease it as speed builds [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

chunks.title: Windshear, wake turbulence and tailwind traps

body.p: Windshear: a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area. It is worst close to the ground and comes with fronts, thunderstorms, inversions and strong winds aloft. A headwind turning into a tailwind drops airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst lasts about 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: On the roll, the only sign may be slower-than-normal airspeed build-up, and gusts can hide it [[28:270|AWH 22-15]].
In studied accidents, the first 5 seconds after lift-off looked normal; the airplane crashed off the end about 20 seconds after lift-off [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

Pilots lowered the nose to regain airspeed and lost altitude. The AWH says this comes from past training emphasis on airspeed control, and recovery needs holding or raising pitch and accepting a lower airspeed [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].
Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to recognize and respond [[28:269|AWH 22-14]]. Some microbursts can't be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

body.p: Teaching point: you are drilling learners to hold VY within a few knots. Explain that a sudden airspeed loss near a storm is the exception, and the real defense is waiting it out on the ground.

Wake turbulence: vortices start when an aircraft rotates [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. They are strongest from an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. They sink several hundred fpm and near the ground drift sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. Short-span airplanes, like trainers, have a harder time countering the roll [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Departing behind a larger aircraft
Note its rotation point, rotate before it, and climb above its path until you turn clear [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before takeoff [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Cross-runway wind of 1 to 5 knots
The upwind vortex can sit on the runway for a while [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]
Want more spacing
Ask for it as soon as practical on ground control, before taxiing onto the runway [[34:155|AIM 7-4-9]]

body.p: Tailwind: a tailwind can move a preceding aircraft's vortices forward into your area, and the light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. It also lengthens the roll (chunk 2).

callout.text: Warning or not, you are expected to adjust your flight path to avoid serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Teach learners that a 'CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE' call is a heads-up, not a plan.

check.q: Why might a well-trained learner make a windshear encounter worse right after lift-off?
check.a: Trained to hold airspeed, they lower the nose to regain it and lose altitude. Recovery needs holding or increasing pitch and accepting lower airspeed [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].

callout.text: At an airport with an operating control tower, no one may operate on a runway or taxiway, or take off or land, without an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].

body.p: Runway incursion: about 65 percent of runway incursions are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by GA pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Runway confusion is more likely with complex airports, runway thresholds close together, and a runway used as a taxiway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Line up and wait (LUAW) is not a takeoff clearance; many pilots have read it back correctly and departed anyway [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]. Before and while taxiing onto the runway, scan its full length, including final and crossing runways [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]].

Collision hazards: in one study of midair collisions, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the accidents. Most happened in good VFR daylight, at or near nontowered airports, below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. If learners think you do all the scanning, they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. In the climb, raise or lower the nose now and then to see over it [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Departing aircraft should watch for arrivals from the opposite direction [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. Landing lights go on with the takeoff clearance, or at the start of the roll at a nontowered field [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

Distractions and task prioritization: many problems start small, like a gauge reading wrong, and pull attention off flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. The sterile flight deck rule is an airline rule, but the AIH says it holds for all pilots and you should model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Loss of situational awareness and disorientation: a rapid acceleration such as a takeoff can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude when visual references are poor, and the pilot may push the nose into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Brief it before the first dark-night or low-visibility departure.

callout.text: Teach learners to take charge: a PIC must know when to tell any passenger, even an examiner, that their actions are interfering with safe flight [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

check.q: Name the three factors that raise the risk of a wrong-runway departure.
check.a: Airport complexity, runway thresholds close together, and joint use of a runway as a taxiway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

chunks.title: Rejected takeoff, engine failure and low-altitude risk

body.p: Rejected takeoff: reasons include a powerplant problem, poor acceleration, a runway incursion or a traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Before takeoff, pick the point where you must be airborne; if you are not, stop at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. To reject: power to idle, maximum braking, keep directional control. For a fire, mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off, and always follow the POH [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Potential engine failure in takeoff/climb phase: you have only seconds. At climb pitch without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, and you may still be holding right rudder. Lower the nose at once, center the rudder, and glide toward a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk choice [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

The FAA turn-back example: failure at 300 feet AGL, 4 seconds to react, a standard-rate turn of 225° takes 75 seconds, and at about 1,000 fpm the airplane ends up 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A turn back is an unacceptable risk for student pilots, low-time and untrained pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Teach learners straight ahead.

Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: 60 percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing, and 20 percent followed an engine failure. Distraction while changing configuration, avoiding traffic or clearing obstacles on takeoff and climb sets them up [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A spin needs a stall plus yaw, and P-factor, torque, wrong rudder and wake all cause yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Power-on stalls are practiced in the takeoff configuration so pilots recognize an accidental stall on takeoff and climb [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

CFIT often follows flight at high density altitude, in mountainous terrain, at night, in low ceilings or visibility, or flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Compare the chart climb rate to the terrain past the runway before you go.

callout.text: Training risk: when you simulate a power failure, one person must clearly have the throttle, since many near accidents came from that confusion. End every simulated emergency approach as soon as the outcome is clear, and never continue it into undue hazard to people or property [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

check.q: Your learner's abort point is 1,500 feet down a 4,000-foot runway. At 1,500 feet the airspeed is still 15 knots short of rotation. What happens next?
check.a: Abort right away: power to idle, maximum braking with directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Inadequate acceleration is a reason to reject [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

body.p: Use the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance under supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. In the airplane it becomes telling-and-doing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Step
In the takeoff lesson
rows: Preparation (on the ground)

Objectives and completion standards, the steps and end result, safety items, and time for questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Brief the abort point, the engine-failure plan and the control exchange [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Instructor tells, instructor does
You fly the takeoff exactly the way the learner will, explaining as you go. If your demo strays from the explanation, say so right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through it while you fly. This catches misunderstandings before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner tells, learner does
The learner flies and talks. You can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill, and you stay ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Assess against the objective; start with the learner's own self-assessment, then yours, with concrete suggestions [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

bullets: Order: taxi crosswind technique comes before crosswind takeoff, a known-to-unknown step [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Follow-through: have the learner ride lightly on the controls, feel the resistance, and see the outside cues while you point them out [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Get it right the first time: primacy means the first habit is the hardest to change [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Insist on correct technique from the start [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Before solo: brief the lighter-airplane takeoff [[24:138|AFH 6-6]], and only let learners practice solo after reasonable competence [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
Use distractions in later lessons, such as asking for the outside air temperature or a field for a forced landing, while the learner holds the climb [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

body.p: Positive exchange of flight controls is critical in this method [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Guard the controls close to the ground. If you need them, calmly say 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain by fighting them for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Which telling-and-doing step lets you find a misunderstanding before the learner is busy flying?
check.a: Learner tells, instructor does: the learner explains while you fly [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: These errors come from the AFH lists for normal takeoffs [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] and crosswind takeoffs [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. The 'what you see' and 'fix' columns use the AFH text around them.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: No POH and chart review
Learner can't state the expected roll or an abort point
Work the chart together before the flight and set the abort point [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Not clearing the area before taxiing onto the runway
No look at final or along the runway
Make 'final clear both ways, runway clear' a spoken habit [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]]
Abrupt throttle
Sharp yaw to the left as power comes in
Smooth, continuous power; the effect is worst in high-horsepower engines [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Not checking engine instruments
Eyes never come inside after power
Add a gauge callout to the roll [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Not anticipating, or overcorrecting, the left turn
Drift left, then S-turns down the runway
Look far ahead at two aligned points; feel pressure, don't make big movements [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Relying only on the airspeed indicator
Head down on the roll; rotation late or early
Teach control feel and outside cues for controllability [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Wrong lift-off attitude
Forced off at high pitch, or nose dropped and it settles
Demonstrate the attitude; learner memorizes it [[24:136|AFH 6-4]] [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Sideslip in the climb
Ball off center, nose yawed
Rudder for torque and P-factor [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Over-controlling elevator, no trim
Pitch wanders; heavy control pressure
Trim off the pressure [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Narrow scan
A wing, usually the left, drops right after lift-off
Step up the outside scan at lift-off; torque rolls the airplane as the wheels leave [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Chasing the airspeed
Airspeed swings above and below VY
Attitude, hold, check [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Less than full aileron into the wind at the start
Upwind wing rises; skipping
Full aileron into the wind at brake release [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]
Mechanical aileron use
Aileron not adjusted as speed builds; drifts off centerline
Judge sideways position from the runway [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Not enough rudder in a crosswind
Nose not parallel to the centerline
Rudder to keep the axis parallel to the centerline [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]
Too much aileron late
Steep bank into the wind at lift-off
Ease aileron as it becomes effective [[24:139|AFH 6-7]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Poor drift correction after lift-off
Track drifts off the extended centerline
Crab into the wind; keep two points in line [[24:140|AFH 6-8]] [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]

body.p: On the checkride, the examiner may play a learner with a simulated error. Name what you see, say the likely cause, demonstrate the fix, then let the 'learner' try again: the same demonstrate, practice, evaluate cycle the AIH uses for reteaching [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Right after lift-off your learner's left wing drops a few degrees every time. Cause and fix?
check.a: A scan limited to straight ahead, plus torque's rolling force as the wheels leave the ground. Fix: wings level and a wider outside scan at lift-off [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

f1.caption: Figure 6-1. Takeoff and climb.
f1.alt: An airplane at four points along a takeoff: takeoff roll at takeoff power, lift-off at takeoff pitch attitude, climb at best climb speed (VY, VX or POH/AFM cruise climb speed), and safe maneuvering altitude at climb power heading into the wind, then en route climb.

f2.caption: Figure 9-7. Steps in the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method, and the telling-and-doing technique compared.
f2.alt: Three columns. Traditional teaching process: preparation, presentation, application, review and evaluation. Demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance supervision, evaluation. Telling-and-doing technique: preparation; instructor tells, instructor does; learner tells, instructor does (highlighted as the key transition); learner tells, learner does; learner does, instructor evaluates.

f3.caption: Figure 6-3. Initial roll and takeoff attitude.
f3.alt: Two side views of a high-wing trainer on a runway with a red horizon reference line. A: initial roll, fuselage level with the horizon. B: takeoff attitude, nosewheel just off the runway and the nose slightly above the horizon.

f4.caption: Figure 11-21. Interpolating charts.
f4.alt: Takeoff distance table for 2,400 lb, flaps 10 degrees, full throttle before brake release, paved level runway, zero wind. Lift-off 51 KIAS, 56 KIAS at 50 feet. Ground roll and total distance over a 50-foot obstacle for sea level to 8,000 feet pressure altitude at 0 to 40 degrees C. Worked example: at 2,500 feet and 20 degrees C, (1,115 + 1,230) / 2 = 1,173 feet ground roll.

f5.caption: Figure 6-6. Crosswind climb flightpath.
f5.alt: Top view of runway 18 with wind blowing from the left. An airplane is shown four times along the centerline: rolling straight, lifting off, then turning its nose into the wind, and finally crabbed with its nose into the wind while its track stays over the extended centerline.

f6.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls.
f6.alt: Three stacked boxes. 1: the instructor says 'You have the flight controls.' 2: the learner acknowledges, 'I have the flight controls.' 3: the instructor again says 'You have the flight controls.' Caption notes a visual check is recommended and the learner keeps flying until the instructor says 'I have the flight controls.'

f7.caption: Figure 18-5. Turning back to the runway after engine failure.
f7.alt: An airplane loses its engine at 300 feet AGL after takeoff, flies a 180-degree turn ending 4,200 feet to the side, then turns to a total of 225 degrees, ending 1,016 feet below runway level.

scenario.title: A gusty first crosswind lesson with an audience
scenario.setup: You are instructing a pre-solo learner in a fixed-gear trainer at a nontowered airport. Runway 36 is 3,200 feet, wet after a shower, with a grass area past the end. Wind is from about 40° left of the runway, gusting. A light twin is doing touch-and-goes on your runway. A towering cumulus is building 15 miles southwest. The learner's friend is watching from the ramp, and the learner badly wants to show off a takeoff.

questions.q: Before you start, what decides whether this runway works today, for this airplane and this learner?
questions.a: The POH distance data for elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]], with room to accelerate and stop: takeoff plus landing ground roll [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Wet pavement can mean hydroplaning on an abort [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Then the learner: does the crosswind fit their personal minimums, not just the airplane's demonstrated value [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]?

questions.q: How do you plan the roll and lift-off for this wind?
questions.a: Full left aileron at the start, easing as speed builds but keeping some in [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. In gusts, stay on the ground a little longer for an extra speed margin, then rotate smoothly and positively [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Climb in a crab on the extended centerline [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

questions.q: The twin just did a touch-and-go. When can you go?
questions.a: Wait at least 2 minutes after a larger aircraft's touch-and-go, especially in light quartering winds, because vortices settle and drift along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Make sure it is not landing over you; watch final both ways [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Convective weather can bring a microburst lasting 5 to 15 minutes [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the roll, the only sign may be slow airspeed build-up [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. If it moves toward the field, wait; some microbursts can't be escaped [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

questions.q: The learner keeps glancing at the ramp. How do you handle the audience?
questions.a: It is a distraction during a critical phase. Brief a sterile flight deck and model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Brief the positive exchange of controls and guard them closely [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: What engine-failure plan do you brief, and will you simulate one today?
questions.a: Abort point on the runway, then if the engine quits after lift-off: nose down, coordinate, land ahead or with a slight turn [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. No turn back for a learner [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. If you simulate a failure later, agree who has the throttle and end it as soon as the outcome is clear [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

skills.do: Complete the before-takeoff and after-takeoff checklists while explaining why each item matters.
skills.practice: Do the flow, then read the checklist as a check, and say aloud why you use it that way [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

skills.do: Make the takeoff radio calls, towered or nontowered, and explain the phraseology.
skills.practice: Script a nontowered departure call with the airport name at both ends [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]] [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Verify the assigned or correct runway before adding power, and explain how you avoid runway confusion.
skills.practice: Heading bug on runway heading; a last check that heading and runway agree [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: Determine wind direction and estimate speed with or without a wind indicator, and teach how.
skills.practice: On every flight, read the wind from the sock and from smoke, dust or water, then compare it with the report [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

skills.do: Position the flight controls for the wind during taxi, lineup and roll, naming each position.
skills.practice: Call out the control position at each turn while taxiing [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]; start every crosswind roll with full aileron into the wind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

skills.do: Clear the area, taxi into position and align on the runway centerline, explaining the references you use.
skills.practice: Scan final and the runway, then pick aligned far references [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]].

skills.do: Advance the throttle smoothly to takeoff power and confirm engine and flight instruments before rotation, saying what you check.
skills.practice: Smooth, continuous throttle; feet off the brakes; gauge callout on the roll [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

skills.do: Rotate and lift off at the recommended airspeed and accelerate to VY, explaining the attitude.
skills.practice: Fly the attitude in Figure 6-3 until you can describe it on the horizon [[24:136|AFH 6-4]].

skills.do: Establish a pitch attitude to maintain the manufacturer’s recommended speed or VY, ±5 knots, while explaining it (ACS AI.VII.A.S12).
skills.practice: Attitude, hold, check, out loud, from the right seat [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane in accordance with manufacturer's guidance and explain flap, gear and power choices.
skills.practice: Brief flap setting and gear-up point before takeoff [[24:236|AFH 12-5]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

skills.do: Maintain VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude while instructing (ACS AI.VII.A.S14).
skills.practice: Practice the patter until it costs you no airspeed; takeoff power to at least 500 feet above obstacles [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Maintain directional control and wind-drift correction through the roll and climb, and explain the crab.
skills.practice: Two points in line ahead; check ground track often in a crosswind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Comply with noise abatement procedures and explain where you found them.
skills.practice: Look up each airport's procedures; when unsure, ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common takeoff errors, usually a simulated error the examiner flies as your 'learner'.
skills.practice: For each error in the table, practice saying what you see, the cause and the fix [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: The demonstration-performance method has how many phases, and what are they?
options: Three: tell, show, do
Four: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with supervision, evaluation
Five: preparation, presentation, application, review, critique
Two: demonstration and evaluation
quiz.why: The AIH divides it into explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

quiz.q: Where does the telling-and-doing technique differ most from the demonstration-performance method?
options: It skips the instructor demonstration
It adds the step 'learner tells, instructor does'
It drops evaluation
It starts with the learner flying
quiz.why: The main difference is the transition 'learner tells, instructor does' between the second and third steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

quiz.q: On the CFI checkride, your POH VY is 79 knots. Which climb airspeed is outside the standard?
options: 75 knots
83 knots
86 knots
79 knots
quiz.why: The Flight Instructor ACS asks for VY ±5 knots, 74 to 84 knots here (ACS AI.VII.A.S14). 86 is 7 knots fast.

quiz.q: A new learner pitches up abruptly just after every lift-off. What does the AFH say the instructor should do?
options: Tell the learner to rotate later
Demonstrate the VY attitude and have the learner memorize it
Teach the takeoff by reference to the airspeed indicator
Use more nose-down trim
quiz.why: The attitude to accelerate to VY should be demonstrated by the instructor and memorized by the learner, who may otherwise hold too much back pressure [[24:136|AFH 6-4]].

quiz.q: Ground effect normally exists up to about what height?
options: One wingspan
Half the fuselage length
50 feet
One-tenth of the wingspan
quiz.why: Ground effect normally occurs up to an altitude equal to one wingspan above the surface [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about the POH flap setting for takeoff?
options: It is a suggestion only
It may be exceeded on short runways
It should never be exceeded
It applies only at gross weight
quiz.why: POH takeoff flap guidance is based on climb performance; under no circumstances should it be exceeded for takeoff [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

quiz.q: What should you tell a learner about the first solo takeoff?
options: It will feel the same
The airplane will lift off earlier and climb faster, and the climb picture may differ
Use more flaps without the instructor's weight
Rotate at a higher speed
quiz.why: With less load the airplane flies sooner and climbs faster, the pitch picture may differ and controls may feel sensitive [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

quiz.q: Per the RMH, flying into an unfamiliar airport suggests adjusting baseline personal minimums by:
options: Adding at least 500 feet to runway length
Adding 5 knots to the wind limit
Subtracting 500 feet from ceiling
No change
quiz.why: The RMH lists adding at least 500 feet to runway length among the extra margins for special conditions such as unfamiliar airports [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, what share of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing?
options: 20 percent
37 percent
60 percent
80 percent
quiz.why: Sixty percent occurred during takeoff and landing, and twenty percent were preceded by engine failure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: During a simulated power failure, what must be clear between you and the learner?
options: Who is talking on the radio
Who has complete control of the throttle
Who reads the checklist
Who chose the landing field
quiz.why: Either the instructor or the learner should have complete control of the throttle; many near accidents came from that confusion [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: You are demonstrating a takeoff and drift a little left of centerline after you just said 'right rudder holds the centerline.' What does the AIH say to do?
options: Ignore it; the learner didn't notice
Acknowledge the deviation and explain it right away
Start the lesson over on the next flight
Let the learner find it in the debrief
final_quiz.why: If the demonstration does not match the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation immediately [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: In 'learner tells, learner does,' your learner says 'nose up to the lift-off attitude at 55,' then raises the nose at 45. What does that most likely show?
options: A misconception about rotation speed
Correct understanding with a skill or timing problem
That the learner should go back to ground school
That the airspeed indicator is wrong
final_quiz.why: Talking while flying shows whether an error comes from a misconception or from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The spoken plan was right, so the problem is in the doing.

final_quiz.q: At 400 feet AGL on climb-out with your learner flying, the engine quits. What is the first priority?
options: Restart attempt with the fuel selector
Turn back toward the runway
Lower the nose immediately and coordinate with rudder
Radio the airport
final_quiz.why: At climb pitch without power the airplane is near a stall; lower the nose and center the rudder, then glide, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: A private-pilot learner asks you to teach the 'impossible turn' so they can use it after a low engine failure. What does the AFH say?
options: Any pilot can do it with a standard-rate turn
It is an unacceptable risk for student and low-time pilots; experienced pilots should train it with an instructor in their make and model
It works whenever the failure is above 300 feet
It is banned by regulation
final_quiz.why: A low turn back is an unacceptable risk for student, low-time and unproficient pilots; experienced pilots should train it with an authorized instructor in the make and model [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: A large airplane landed on your runway a minute ago. The wind is a 3-knot crosswind. Why is that a concern?
options: Light crosswinds speed up vortex decay
A 1 to 5 knot cross-runway wind can keep the upwind vortex in place on the runway
Vortices only form on takeoff
Crosswinds lift vortices above the pattern
final_quiz.why: A light cross-runway wind of 1 to 5 knots can leave the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone for a while [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

final_quiz.q: Why might a pilot trained to hold VY within a few knots react badly to a windshear airspeed loss after lift-off?
options: They will add too much power
Training emphasis on airspeed control leads them to lower the nose, giving up altitude
They will retract flaps too early
They will level off too high
final_quiz.why: Reducing pitch to regain airspeed is the result of past training emphasis on airspeed control; recovery needs holding or increasing pitch [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to lower both their crosswind and ceiling personal minimums before a trip next week. Best advice per the RMH?
options: Lower both now to save time
Change one variable at a time, not to make a specific flight, after training with an instructor
Personal minimums can't be changed
Use the airplane's demonstrated crosswind instead
final_quiz.why: Don't adjust minimums to complete a specific flight, change one variable at a time, and consult an instructor first [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: On a crosswind roll your learner's airplane makes a series of small bounces while sliding sideways. What is it, and why stop it?
options: Porpoising; it overheats the brakes
Side-skipping; it puts severe side loads on the gear and can break it
Wheelbarrowing; it only wears the tires
Normal; it happens in every crosswind
final_quiz.why: Skipping develops into side-skipping, which can cause structural failure of the gear; it comes from improper aileron use [[24:139|AFH 6-7]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH want the learner to sense control resistance during the takeoff roll?
options: It shows airspeed more accurately than the indicator
It shows the degree of controllability, not speed
It reduces wear on the tires
It is required by the ACS
final_quiz.why: The feel of resistance is not a measure of speed but of controllability; the learner should sense pressure, not chase movement [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

final_quiz.q: A dark-night takeoff over unlit terrain: just after lift-off the learner says 'we're climbing too steeply' and pushes forward. What may be happening?
options: Ground effect
Somatogravic illusion from the takeoff acceleration
Carburetor ice
Adverse yaw
final_quiz.why: Rapid acceleration can create a false nose-up feeling with poor visual references, and the pilot may push into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a light single from a field with a formal runway use program. Does 14 CFR 91.129(h) require you to use the assigned noise runway?
options: Yes, every aircraft must
The rule binds large or turbine airplanes, but you should still follow published procedures and fly quietly
Only at night
Only if the tower says 'noise abatement'
final_quiz.why: 91.129(h) applies to large or turbine-powered airplanes [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(h)]]. All pilots should be considerate and use the airport's procedures, asking the tower if unsure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Which group lists the three major factors that raise the risk of runway confusion?
options: Night, rain, fatigue
Airport complexity, close runway thresholds, a runway used as a taxiway
Tower closed, no ATIS, crosswind
Long runways, displaced thresholds, lights out
final_quiz.why: The PHAK names airport complexity, close proximity of thresholds and joint use of a runway as a taxiway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing through 100 feet, your startled learner freezes on the yoke and pulls. What does the AIH say about taking control?
options: Talk them through it while both stay on the controls
Take the controls, calmly say 'I have the flight controls,' and don't fight an anxious learner for control
Wait until they let go
Reduce power first
final_quiz.why: When needed, take control and calmly announce it; anxious learners can be very strong, and nothing is gained by having them on the controls during a recovery [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

takeaways: You fly to VY ±5 knots and explain it at the same time; your learner is held to +10/-5 on the private checkride.
Predict the roll with the POH and personal minimums; the airplane's limit is not the learner's limit [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].
Teach with telling-and-doing; 'learner tells, instructor does' catches misunderstandings early [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Demonstrate the lift-off and VY attitude and have the learner memorize it [[24:136|AFH 6-4]].
Build crosswind takeoff on taxi technique: full aileron into the wind, less as speed builds, then crab.
Brief the abort point, a straight-ahead engine-failure plan and the control exchange every time.
Guard the controls close to the ground, and take them calmly with 'I have the flight controls.'
cfi_notes: If no crosswind exists on test day, the examiner must test crosswind knowledge orally (ACS AI.VII.A Note). Have a crosswind explanation ready with the taxi-to-takeoff link.

The AFH chapter 6 instructor notes are gold for this Task: follow-through on the controls [[24:135|AFH 6-3]], demonstrating the attitude [[24:136|AFH 6-4]], two tracking points and the solo briefing [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Quote them.

The sources are silent on how to simulate an engine failure during a single-engine takeoff roll or low climb. The AFH technique of introducing failures with a smooth throttle reduction and pulling a mixture on the roll is written for multiengine training [[24:284|AFH 13-35]]. Follow your school's SOP and the AFH single-engine guidance on throttle control and ending simulations early [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

The AWH windshear studies are about large airplanes flown by crews (it talks about tail strikes and V-speeds) [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. Its pitch lesson still applies, but it gives no step-by-step escape for light singles.
Figure 11-21 is a sample table with flaps 10° and zero wind [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. Make learners read the conditions box on their own POH chart before they read a number.
The AFH uses 'student'; the AIH uses 'learner'. Same person. The CFI ACS asks you to demonstrate and explain at once, so practice the patter until it costs no airspeed.
Habit transfer cuts both ways: drilling airspeed precision can produce the wrong windshear reaction [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]. Tell learners where the rule changes.
AIH collision study: an instructor was on board in 37 percent of midairs [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Say it out loud on the first lesson so the learner owns the scan.
gaps: Exact speeds (rotation, VX, VY, cruise climb), flap settings, maximum demonstrated crosswind and leaning procedure are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No source defines 'safe maneuvering altitude'; the AFH only recommends takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
No single-engine source gives a method or minimum altitude for simulated engine failures right after takeoff; that is a CFI and school SOP decision.
AC 00-54 (FAA Pilot Wind Shear Guide), named by the PHAK [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], is not in the resources.
Airport-specific noise abatement procedures and declared distances are in the Chart Supplement, which is not in the resources.

Learner's first solo, instructor's weight gone

activities.title: Runway math with Figure 11-21
activities.intro: Use the table in Figure 11-21 and the rules in the lesson, then type your answer.

items.q: Ground roll at 3,500 feet pressure altitude and 30 °C (interpolate)?
items.why: Average the 3,000-foot and 4,000-foot ground rolls at 30 °C: (1,325 + 1,465) / 2 = 1,395 feet [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

items.q: Total distance over a 50-foot obstacle at 5,000 feet and 20 °C, plus the RMH pilot's 20% personal margin?
items.why: The table gives 2,895 feet [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. 2,895 x 1.2 = 3,474 feet, using the 20% margin from the RMH example [[30:32|RMH 3-14]].

items.q: Take the 1,395-foot ground roll and add a tailwind of 10% of takeoff speed. About how long now?
items.why: A 10% tailwind adds about 21%: 1,395 x 1.21 = 1,688 feet [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: Ground roll at 2,000 feet and 20 °C is in the table; the POH landing ground roll is 600 feet. Estimate the runway needed to accelerate and stop.
items.why: 1,115 feet from the table [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]] plus 600 = 1,715 feet; takeoff plus landing ground roll is the AFH estimate [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

items.q: A trainer's VSO is 48 knots. Up to what 90° crosswind was it shown controllable in certification?

activities.title: True or false: eyes outside
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In an AIH study, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of midair collisions.
cards.why: True [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Instructors are not a guarantee of seeing traffic.

cards.s: Most midair collisions happen in poor visibility.
cards.why: False. Most happen in daylight with visibility greater than 3 miles [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

cards.s: Most midair collisions happen at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet.
The sterile flight deck rule is for airlines only, so it has nothing to teach a GA learner.
cards.why: False. The AIH says it holds for the whole aviation community and instructors should model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

cards.s: Before taxiing onto the runway for line up and wait, you should scan the full length of the runway, including crossing runways and final.
Turn on landing lights as soon as you enter the runway for line up and wait.
cards.why: False. All lights except landing lights; landing lights go on with the takeoff clearance [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

activities.title: First crosswind lesson
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your pre-solo learner has done normal takeoffs, and today has a steady left crosswind within limits. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On the ground before the flight, what goes in your briefing?
options: Just 'we'll figure it out in the air'
Objectives, standards, steps and safety items, the abort point, and how you will exchange controls
Only the crosswind component
A quiz on regulations
steps.why: The explanation phase covers objectives, standards, steps, end result and safety [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; the preflight brief includes the control exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] and the abort point [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

steps.s: First crosswind takeoff of the day. Who flies it?
options: The learner, to see what happens
You, explaining as you fly, with the learner following lightly on the controls
You, silently, so the learner can watch
Nobody; do it in the simulator only
steps.why: Instructor tells, instructor does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], with the learner following through lightly and feeling the pressures [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

steps.s: Learner's turn. At 30 knots the left wing starts to lift. What do you say?
options: 'More left aileron, into the wind'
'Right aileron, level the wings'
'Pull back and fly it off'
'Brake on the right'
steps.why: Hold aileron into the wind to keep the upwind wing down; a rising upwind wing can lead to skipping [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

steps.s: At 50 feet the learner yanks the nose up and the stall horn sounds. What now?
options: Let the learner work it out
Calmly say 'I have the flight controls,' take control and lower the nose to the climb attitude
Talk them through it while both of you pull
Reduce power
steps.why: Take control when necessary and announce it calmly [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Too much back pressure makes the angle of attack excessive and can stall the airplane [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

steps.s: Back on the ground. How do you start the debrief?
options: List every mistake first
Ask the learner to assess their own takeoffs, then compare with yours and give concrete suggestions
Skip it; the flight was short
Tell them they are not ready for solo
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with learner self-assessment, then the instructor's; offer concrete help and avoid ending on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
